content:
The scariest part about burnout:

You mistake it for "drive."

For my first 12 years on Wall Street, I ran on fumes.

Coffee. 
Determination. 
The occasional vacation that barely moved the needle.

But underneath it all - 
A growing level of exhaustion and anxiety 
I justified as the price you pay for "being driven."

I told everyone I was fine.

I told myself: once I get the promotion, it'll ease up.

But as I climbed the ranks, it only got worse.

Maybe you've felt the same.

Giving more than you're putting back in.
Running a deficit you can't seem to close.

Here's what I wish I'd known sooner:

Managing your energy isn't about controlling who gets it.
It's just math.

You don't have to protect every drop.
You just have to take in more than you give away.

If you want to do the same audit I did:

1/ Create two columns: takers and givers. 
→ Write them down. Follow your gut; don't overthink it.

2/ Delete one energy taker
→ Pick the easiest one. Remove it for a week.

3/ Add one energy giver
→ Start small. One walk. One break. One week.

That's it.

You don't have to overhaul your entire life.
You just have to change one thing at a time.

Meditation became my one energy giver 
that refilled the tank daily.
